summary: Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations for Aurora's high-concurrency customer support retrieval use case. Discussed cache hit-rate sensitivity, cost tradeoffs (tokens/GPU time), recommended configs for hosted vs Dedicated, and pilot benchmarking plan.
topics: Overview of Redwood Optimize features (batching, KV/prefix cache)
Cost model walkthrough and example math
Hit-rate vs TTL tradeoffs and security considerations
Dedicated vs Hosted economics and fallback policies
Pilot benchmark plan and next steps
questions: What's acceptable p95 latency for your interactive use case?
How much of the corpus is static vs frequently updated?
Do you require customer-managed KMS for KV cache encryption?
transcript:
00:00:00 - Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samir from Redwood, this is Jenna our solutions engineer and Omar product. quick introductions?
00:00:08 - Maya Chen: hi, Maya here, Head of ML at Aurora Finance, thanks for squeezing us in.
00:00:12 - Rohit Singh: Rohit, platform eng, mostly infra and cost decisions.
00:00:15 - Elena Garcia: Elena, CTO, will chime on security and timelines.
00:00:20 - Samir Patel: Awesome. Agenda real quick: walkthrough Optimize recommendations — batching and prefix/KV cache — then cost model examples and a proposed pilot. Any constraints up front?
00:00:30 - Luis Ortega: Our primary constraint is p95 under 400ms for support chat flows, and we have spikes up to 600 rps. Also strict data residency and KMS.
00:00:40 - Jenna Ruiz: Got it. We'll shape recommendations around that. quick note — transcription might mis-hear some infra names, sorry in advance.
00:00:48 - Omar Haddad: I'll jump in on the product parts.
00:00:50 - Samir Patel: Ok starting with batching basics: Redwood's continuous batching pools requests into micro-batches shorter than a second to improve throughput. For interactive webchat we tune target latency and max batch size. Example: with your p95 400ms we recommend target batch latency of ~60ms and max batch size tuned to expected concurrency. That usually gives 2-3x token cost reduction vs naive single-request mode.
00:01:20 - Rohit Singh: When you say 2-3x reduction, that's per-token or per-request? how does that translate to GPU utilization?
00:01:28 - Jenna Ruiz: Good question. It's mostly per-token effective cost because batching amortizes attention computation and kernel setup. In practice GPU cycles per token drop because we increase throughput; e.g., a 16-token average request at 100 concurrent users could reduce per-token cost ~2.2x depending on sequence lengths.
00:01:45 - Maya Chen: Sequence lengths are bimodal for us — short prompts ~20 tokens plus retrieval context usually 400-1,200 tokens. So long tails exist.
00:01:53 - Jenna Ruiz: That's important — long sequences change batching efficiency. We recommend two things: prefix (KV) cache for the retrieval context so you only generate on the dynamic prompt, and smart bucketing by sequence length so long requests don't block small ones. Redwood supports both at the routing level.
00:02:12 - Samir Patel: moving to KV/prefix cache: conceptually we cache the KV states for the encoder/decoder for repeated prefixes (retrieved docs). If you can hit 60-70% on the KV cache for the large context, you'll see major token savings because the model doesn't re-compute the full context every request.
00:02:29 - Rohit Singh: what's a realistic hit rate for retrieval-augmented support flows?
00:02:33 - Jenna Ruiz: Depends on retrieval quality & TTL. With stable docs and deterministic retrieval, we often see 50-75% hit rates. If docs update frequently or you have per-customer personalization in the prefix, hit rates fall. Also note the cold-start cost for loading KV into GPU memory when a new prefix appears. That's why TTL and pre-warming matter.
00:02:50 - Elena Garcia: Security question — is KV cache encrypted at rest and can it be customer-managed KMS?
00:02:55 - Omar Haddad: Yes, for Private deployments and Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS for cache encryption. For hosted we provide encryption and audited access logs; we can share SOC2 docs. We'll drop the exact security link after the call.
00:03:06 - Samir Patel: let's walk through a short cost example (math on the call): assume baseline (no batching, no cache) per-request average tokens generated 600, model cost X per token on a GPU. With 50% KV hit we only generate 300 tokens, and with batching you reduce effective token/GPU time by another ~30-40% for these request patterns. so net you'd see ~65-70% reduction in GPU time per request.
00:03:35 - Rohit Singh: can you give numbers referencing our expected 600 rps spike? how many GPUs roughly?
00:03:40 - Jenna Ruiz: Quick back-of-envelope: if your avg tokens per request after prefix caching is 300 and after batching effective per-token GPU cost is 0.0009 GPU-seconds, at 600 rps that's 180 GPU-seconds per second, so 1 GPU of type A can do ~X GPU-seconds — (transcription note: SE said 'a100 like 300' maybe misheard). Rough numbers: depending on GPU type and model quantization, you'd need 4-8 GPUs for steady sustained 600rps with interactive latency SLOs. We will run a dedicated bench to give exact counts.
00:04:10 - Maya Chen: how do you handle cache invalidation on doc updates? we often have content that changes hourly and some docs are session-specific.
00:04:17 - Jenna Ruiz: we recommend TTLs per collection and a versioned prefix key. For high-change docs, TTLs of a few minutes or avoid caching. For stable collections, longer TTLs. Also policy: on writes you can trigger invalidation via API, or use a short TTL plus warm-up. We showed a flow in the docs — will share link.
00:04:34 - Samir Patel: tradeoff is simple: higher hit rate lowers cost but increases risk of stale outputs. For finance data with updates, probably hybrid approach.
00:04:42 - Luis Ortega: Does warm-up cause spikes in GPU memory or extra API calls we should be aware of?
00:04:46 - Omar Haddad: Warm-up means pre-loading KV states which is a one-time GPU memory and compute cost; Redwood supports pre-warm orchestration to schedule during low-traffic windows and limit burst. We can attach warm-up to your rollout pipeline.
00:04:58 - Samir Patel: quick note on Dedicated vs Hosted: Dedicated lets you pin capacity and use customer KMS and VPC peering — good for regulated workloads and predictable cost. Hosted is simpler and autoscaled but has some limits on KMS and private networking depending on region. For your compliance needs I'd expect we look at Private or Dedicated.
00:05:16 - Elena Garcia: timeline for Private? we have procurement cycles.
00:05:19 - Samir Patel: Private typically 8-12 weeks for an initial deployment with a dedicated control plane and on-prem options; Dedicated is faster, 2-4 weeks depending on contract. We'll confirm with the solutions team and include in the follow-up.
00:05:28 - Rohit Singh: on cost model spreadsheet — will you include quantized model variants and savings?
00:05:33 - Jenna Ruiz: yes, we'll include LP4/INT8 quantized variants, price multipliers, and the expected latency/quality tradeoff. Also model fallbacks — if a quantized variant misses quality we can route to larger model for that route.
00:05:46 - Samir Patel: let's talk about an experiment/pilot: propose 1) mirror traffic for 24-48h to Redwood's pilot cluster (non-prod data) to measure real hit rates and latency; 2) run two phases: baseline (no cache/batching tuning) then optimized (prefix cache + batching config), collect token/GPU metrics.
00:06:02 - Maya Chen: That sounds good. what's required from us?
00:06:05 - Jenna Ruiz: We'll need traffic replay or a 7-day histogram, model version you want to test (open model name), and a list of routes with PII requirements so we can set cache TTLs and encryption. Also an SSO account for access.
00:06:18 - Rohit Singh: We'll provide histogram and SRE contacts. Also, question: how do you measure KV cache hit/miss in the dashboard?
00:06:24 - Omar Haddad: In Redwood Console Optimize tab we have per-route hit-rate, miss-rate, average TTL, and token savings. We can send screenshots. There's also an API to export event-level debugging logs.
00:06:36 - Samir Patel: we typically target a pilot budget estimate; ballpark — for a 48h mirrored run at your expected spike scaled down to 30% production, pilot cluster cost might be in the low thousands USD; exact numbers in the sheet.
00:06:49 - Elena Garcia: procurement will ask for benchmarks vs AWS. Any issues running the benchmark in our cloud?
00:06:53 - Jenna Ruiz: We can run on Redwood Hosted or spin a Dedicated pilot in your VPC (we support marketplace images or partner infra). We'll include exact runner options.
00:07:02 - Luis Ortega: Do you support per-customer isolation in cache keys? we don't want cross-tenant leakage.
00:07:07 - Jenna Ruiz: Yes, prefix keys can be namespaced per-tenant and encryption & RBAC prevent cross-tenant access. We'll include recommended key naming schemes.
00:07:16 - Samir Patel: ok quick recap of next steps: Samir sends cost model + config, Jenna schedules pilot & shares the dashboard screenshots, Aurora provides traffic histogram and list of PII routes. Any other items?
00:07:28 - Maya Chen: can you also include a short blurb on fallback behavior if cache miss + latency spike? we want to avoid timeouts.
00:07:33 - Omar Haddad: We'll include recommended fallback policies: route to lower-latency quantized model or fall back to a cached short answer, and circuit-breaker thresholds in the Console.
00:07:42 - Samir Patel: Great. I'll email the docs and cost spreadsheet after the call. Thanks everyone.
00:07:48 - Elena Garcia: Thanks, appreciate the detail.
00:07:50 - Rohit Singh: Thanks all.
00:07:52 - Maya Chen: Thanks.
00:07:55 - End of recording (approx 56 minutes)
